bookArc.proposal: Present the book as a 120-page analytical history rather than a lead magnet: twelve source-conscious chapters, one sustained Nineveh case, one close reading of a single document, and a final bounded synthesis.
bookArc.question: How have changing social, material, and political conditions shaped the forms and scale of human aggression across history?

premise: A source-conscious historical survey of human aggressiveness across eras and regions, examining how social organization, resources, institutions, culture, technology, and circumstance have influenced both violence and restraint. The book distinguishes individual aggression from organized warfare and treats the surviving evidence as uneven rather than as a simple story of progress or decline.
audience: General readers curious about history who want a clear, balanced account of human aggression across eras and regions.

chapters.title: What Counts as Aggression?
chapters.summary: Establish the book's distinctions and open with early physical evidence while showing why the historical record cannot provide a simple timeline of human violence.
keyBeats: Open with a healed injury on an ancient human skull and the limited conclusions that injury permits.
Distinguish aggression, interpersonal violence, organized warfare, coercion, and defensive action.
Introduce the survival bias of archaeological and written evidence.
Set up the central question: which social and material conditions alter the expression of aggression?

chapters.title: Before Armies and Kingdoms
chapters.summary: Examine evidence from mobile communities and early settlements without treating either way of life as uniformly peaceful or violent.
keyBeats: Present the Nataruk remains as evidence of a specific violent encounter, with careful attention to what the site cannot establish.
Compare individual conflict, small-scale raiding, and organized warfare as different historical problems.
Consider mobility, food storage, kinship, and access to territory as possible conditions affecting conflict.
Show how sparse remains make population-wide claims difficult.

chapters.title: Fields, Surplus, and Unequal Power
chapters.summary: Trace how settled agriculture and stored resources changed the opportunities for coercion, while resisting a single-cause account of violence.
keyBeats: Introduce stored food, fixed settlements, and property claims as new objects of protection and contest.
Explain why agricultural expansion may correlate with some forms of conflict without proving a universal increase.
Examine emerging inequality and dependence through concrete settlement and burial evidence.
End with the distinction between conditions that permit violence and motives that justify it.

chapters.title: Bronze, Walls, and the First States
chapters.summary: Follow the institutional growth of warfare through fortified places, weapons, administration, and political authority in the ancient Near East and neighboring regions.
keyBeats: Introduce fortified settlements and weapon technologies as material signs of organized threat.
Show how rulers used records, taxation, labor, and public monuments to organize coercive power.
Read royal victory narratives alongside their purpose as political documents.
Compare the administrative capacity of states with the uneven experience of people living under them.

chapters.title: Law, Punishment, and the Authorized Blow
chapters.summary: Read legal and political documents as records of both violence and attempts to regulate it.
keyBeats: Open with a surviving legal provision concerning injury, status, or compensation.
Distinguish law's description of violence from law's authorization of punishment.
Examine how rank, gender, citizenship, enslavement, and household authority shaped whose aggression counted as legitimate.
Show how formal restraint can coexist with severe institutional violence.

chapters.title: A City at War: The Siege of Nineveh
chapters.summary: Narrate one extended case of organized violence through the Assyrian imperial record, material remains, and the limits of victorious testimony. The chapter treats the siege and its aftermath as a single case rather than as a general survey.
keyBeats: Locate Nineveh within the Assyrian imperial system and its relationship to tributary communities.
Introduce the royal inscriptions and reliefs as deliberate instruments of intimidation and memory.
Follow the movement from mobilization and siege to capture, punishment, deportation, and administrative incorporation.
Contrast the empire's self-presentation with the silences and partial traces left by defeated populations.
Identify what this case reveals about communication, fear, logistics, and state power without generalizing to all ancient warfare.

chapters.title: A Letter from the Frontier
chapters.summary: Read one historical document closely as a window onto fear, obligation, and local conflict, keeping the document's perspective and missing context visible.
keyBeats: Introduce a single frontier letter or administrative report and identify its author, recipient, date, and survival context when securely known.
Follow the document's immediate concern: threat, retaliation, desertion, requisition, or protection.
Separate the writer's description from the historian's interpretation.
End with the unanswered questions created by the document's narrow viewpoint.

chapters.title: Honor, Kinship, and Retaliation
chapters.summary: Examine how social reputation, kin obligations, feud, and reconciliation could intensify or contain aggression in different historical settings.
keyBeats: Introduce honor as a local social relationship rather than a timeless psychological trait.
Show how kinship could support retaliation and also impose duties of mediation.
Compare a documented feud or dispute with institutions that redirected revenge into compensation or arbitration.
Explain how gendered expectations and social rank shaped public interpretations of insult and response.
Keep the comparison bounded by differences in sources and social organization.

chapters.title: Religion, Rule, and the Moral Naming of Enemies
chapters.summary: Explore how religious and political language classified violence, sacrifice, punishment, conquest, and defense without reducing belief to a simple cause of war.
keyBeats: Introduce a concrete inscription, ritual setting, sermon, or legal text that assigns moral meaning to conflict.
Distinguish religious justification from the logistical and political conditions that made violence possible.
Examine how enemy categories were created and how insiders were disciplined.
Show cases where religious institutions restrained violence as well as cases where they authorized it.

chapters.title: Guns, Empires, and Distant Violence
chapters.summary: Trace how expanding empires, firearms, commerce, bureaucracy, and racial classification altered the scale and distance of coercion in the early modern and modern worlds.
keyBeats: Open with a weapon, map, ledger, or administrative order that connects distant decisions to local violence.
Show how technology changes capacity without determining political use.
Examine colonial classification, forced labor, displacement, or state punishment through a documented case.
Distinguish battlefield violence from structural coercion and the limits of retrospective comparison.

chapters.title: The Twentieth Century's Uneven Record
chapters.summary: Assess mass warfare, genocide, state terror, and changing civilian exposure while avoiding a single verdict that the modern age is simply more or less violent.
keyBeats: Introduce one documented episode through survivor testimony, official records, or material evidence with clear provenance.
Explain how industrial administration and communication could expand the reach of violence.
Contrast mass mobilization with efforts to regulate war and protect civilians.
Address why casualty counts, archives, and political memory produce different pictures of the period.

chapters.title: What Changes Aggression?
chapters.summary: Synthesize the cases into a cautious account of how institutions, resources, social learning, technology, ecology, and historical memory shape aggressive behavior and organized violence.
keyBeats: Compare the distinct mechanisms introduced across the book rather than repeating every case.
Clarify what the historical record supports about context-sensitive aggression and what remains unresolved.
Separate biological capacity from social activation, political organization, and moral permission.
Return to the opening question with a bounded answer that preserves variation across eras and regions.
Close with the practical historical insight that restraint is built, contested, and vulnerable rather than automatic.

promises: The book will distinguish human capacity for aggression from the historical conditions that activate, organize, or restrain it.
The Nataruk evidence will be interpreted cautiously rather than used as proof of a universal prehistoric pattern.
The long Nineveh case will show how organized violence depends on institutions, communication, logistics, and representation.
A single historical document will reveal both the value and the severe limits of close reading.
The conclusion will explain what can be said across eras and regions without pretending that one trend fits all cases.

openingHook: At Nataruk, on the shore of Kenya's Lake Turkana, a human skeleton preserves the trace of a violent encounter that ended thousands of years ago. The injury raises a question the bone cannot answer by itself: what conditions turned conflict into an attack?

authorStance.thesis: Human aggression takes many forms, but its scale and direction are shaped decisively by the social arrangements, material pressures, institutions, and meanings through which people live.
refusals: I refuse to describe whole peoples or periods as naturally violent or naturally peaceful.
I refuse to turn one archaeological site or written account into a measure of humanity as a whole.
I refuse to end a chapter with a symmetrical list of causes when the evidence supports a more specific conclusion.
I refuse to use graphic suffering as a substitute for historical explanation.
positions: People have long possessed both the capacity for aggression and the capacity for cooperation.
Organized violence becomes more durable when institutions can gather resources, assign enemies, and reward or compel participation.
Material pressure can intensify conflict, but it does not determine whether communities choose attack, negotiation, flight, or restraint.
Laws, rituals, kinship systems, and political authorities can restrain violence while also legitimizing particular forms of coercion.
authorStance.voiceSample: In 1919, the harbor at Trieste held ships bearing flags from several vanished empires. A customs ledger from that spring recorded crates of coffee, bolts of cloth, and the names of officials learning a new border. Near the rail yard, a Slovenian-speaking porter carried a paper stamped by an Italian office that could not read his surname correctly. The error occupied one line in the document, while the delay kept his wages from reaching his family on time. At the same station, a newspaper described the city as a prize secured by sacrifice. The phrase belonged to a public argument about sovereignty, yet the ledger offered a quieter record of sovereignty's daily cost. A blue pencil marked one consignment for inspection. A clerk folded the page beside a brass scale. In the following months, police reports, party notices, and school regulations gave the new order a sharper outline. Each document named a different city, although the streets remained the same. The harbor's cranes lifted cargo above the roofs, and the customs office translated political change into stamps, queues, and withheld permissions. A map printed in Rome placed Trieste inside a nation; the porter’s delayed pay placed the nation inside an ordinary household. Neither paper settled what the city would become. Together, they showed how power entered a place through objects small enough to fit in a clerk’s hand.

pageRules: Use illustration only when a specific artifact, place, document, map, or process can clarify the page.
When Nataruk appears, label the scene with the exact place name and avoid inventing reconstructed faces or motives.
When Nineveh appears, use the exact location name and distinguish reconstructed architecture from verified remains.
Do not depict unnamed historical populations with stereotyped clothing, facial features, or generic ethnic markers.
Prefer diagrams, maps, document details, and site plans for analytical pages.
Do not include text inside images unless the image is a clearly labeled map, diagram, inscription, or document detail.
Avoid graphic injury and spectacle; show scale, setting, objects, and institutional processes instead.
Keep visual chronology and material culture consistent with the chapter's period.

illustrationPlan.globalStyle: Documentary historical illustration with restrained color, accurate material details, clear geographic and chronological cues, and no sensationalized gore. Use maps, artifacts, settlement plans, documents, and archaeological scenes when they clarify the argument.
